name: Reporting to Families
title: Reporting to Families
answer: Reporting to Families is about giving families clear, timely information about their child's progress so they can help. It matters because weekly messages about missed work, grades, and absences reduced course failures and raised math scores in the cited trials, and because families who understand assessment data can act as partners. AI can help translate data into plain explanations, but teachers and human reviewers check critical information.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Families need to know how children are doing in plain language and early enough to help. The problem is that raw assessment data, such as a percentile score, often does not tell parents what their child is strong in or what needs practice. Reporting to families solves this by turning data into family friendly progress reports that explain meaning rather than only listing numbers. AI can assist in converting data into clear explanations, and the teacher checks them. This puts assessment data to use in a way families can understand and act on.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not give grade bands. It describes progress reports that explain what data means, for example a child is strong in fractions and needs practice with word problems. Student information system portals and messaging tools such as TalkingPoints can deliver these reports in families' languages. The translation rules from Chapter 14 apply. Critical information about a child's progress deserves human review in the family's language. Families who understand the data can become partners in acting on it.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels these as among the strongest findings in this Volume. It cites trials in which weekly messages about missed assignments, grades, and absences cut course failures by 27 percent (Bergman et al., 2021). It also cites raised math scores in Chile (Berlinski et al., 2021). The text presents these as evidence that family friendly progress reports put assessment data to work. No other studies, figures, or findings are given in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: AI can help turn data into clear explanations, but the teacher checks them. The translation rules from Chapter 14 apply. Critical information about a child's progress deserves human review in the family's language. The decisions about what to report and how to act stay with people, not with the AI. The text does not set out additional limits or risks beyond these review and translation requirements.
